title: Filmation sprite sheet
description: A remake's graphics: the sprites themselves, what each is called, and the table saying how every graphic number is drawn. Written ONCE by sprite_sheet.py out of the extraction; nothing regenerates it, so it is the authoritative source the game is built from and is meant to be edited.

game.description: The build's half of the atlas; the graphics panel ignores it.

graphicCount.description: How many graphic numbers the game HAS, which is not how many it uses: sprite_table has to be this long or a room naming a graphic past the end would read off it. 256 for Knight Lore, 172 for Pentagram.

graphics.description: Graphic number -> how it is drawn. A number that is not here is one the game does not use. Several numbers may point at one sprite -- that is the game's own doing -- but they are NOT interchangeable, because the nudge below is per graphic number: Knight Lore's 30 and 150 draw the same bitmap four rows apart.

propertyNames.description: A graphic number, in decimal, below `count`.

name.description: What this graphic is CALLED. rooms.json refers to graphics by these names. It is seeded from the sprite that draws it the first time sprite_sheet.py writes the file and then belongs to the graphic, so pointing the graphic at a different sprite changes what it draws and does NOT rename it -- every castle that places it keeps working.

sprite.description: Which bitmap draws it: an index into the sprite sheet's `sprites` list, in the order sprite_data.bin holds them. 255 is not a sprite -- it is what the packed form used for 'no bitmap', and here you leave the key out instead. A graphic can have a nudge and no sprite; Knight Lore's 1 does.

x.description: Pixels right. object_place ADDS this to the left edge, so a negative value moves the artwork left. Harvested from a running game by adj.py -- the game picks these inside its per-graphic update routines rather than reading a table, so editing one by hand means disagreeing with the original on purpose.

y.description: Pixels up. object_place SUBTRACTS this from the base row, because the artwork's Y is bottom-up and the screen's is not.

mirrored.description: The nudge to use when the piece is drawn the other way round. Given only where it differs from the plain one -- four graphics in each game want a different nudge mirrored, and everything else uses the one pair either way.

note.description: Where a nudge came from, when adj.py borrowed it rather than harvesting it -- a body facing the game never shows takes its other side's.

nudge.description: A signed byte: the game does this arithmetic in eight bits.
